title: The Sharpe Pint: Notepad Leaks, Asymmetric Shorts, and the Big Muddy

opening_mood.text: Morning. If you spent your weekend bracing for a geopolitical meltdown in the Middle East, Monday's markets probably felt like a cold pint of lager after a long shift. Between Donald Trump calling off strikes on Iran and a rare, coordinated US-Japan currency intervention, risk-on sentiment is back with a vengeance.

Grab your coffee; we have a lot to unpack today, from Scott Bessent's leaked notepad to the beautiful, risk-free world of the Greenshoe option, and why asking an LLM to time the market is like asking a very eloquent English graduate to fly a Harrier Jump Jet.

content.text: The Great Yen Squeeze: Coordinated Intervention Defends the Treasury Market

Late last week, the US and Japan pulled off a rare, coordinated yen-buying intervention to rescue the Japanese currency from a 40-year low of almost 164 to the dollar. The yen immediately surged to around 155-157. Japan's Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed the joint action, warning they will not hesitate to do it again. Estimates suggest Japan spent a record-breaking $34 billion on Friday (on top of $53 billion solo on Thursday), while the US chipped in a symbolic but highly effective $5-10 billion.

Why does this matter? It is the first coordinated intervention to strengthen the yen in nearly 30 years. For months, the massive interest rate gap between the US and Japan has fueled the yen carry trade. This intervention is a direct shot across the bow of those speculators. The real story here isn't just the yen; it's a defensive shield for the US Treasury market. Japan is the largest foreign holder of US debt ($1.14 trillion). If Tokyo had to keep intervening solo, it would have to dump US Treasuries to raise dollars, sending already high US yields screaming upward. By stepping in and utilizing the Fed's FIMA repo facility, the US has managed to stabilize the yen without triggering a bond market bloodbath.

items: What to say at work: The US-Japan intervention is basically a Treasury protection racket. The Fed and Treasury stepped in because they couldn't afford Japan dumping billions of Treasuries into an already tight bond market to defend the yen.

content.text: Palantir's Blowout: AI Software is Actually Making Money

Palantir (PLTR) just delivered the kind of quarter that a stock priced for perfection rarely gets. Q2 revenue surged 93% year-on-year to $1.935 billion (beating estimates of $1.81 billion), and GAAP net income hit $1.062 billion—a staggering 55% margin. The standout was US commercial revenue, which grew 149% YoY to $764 million. Management raised its full-year revenue guidance to over $8.15 billion, sending the stock up 12-15% in after-hours trading.

Why does this matter? For months, the big question hanging over the AI trade has been: Is anyone actually making money from software, or is it just Nvidia selling hardware? Palantir's results are the clearest proof yet that enterprise AI software can scale and generate massive cash flow. This is a major validation for growth managers who have been sweating over tech valuations. Palantir is proving it can convert AI pilots into massive, multi-million dollar enterprise contracts, shifting the narrative from infrastructure spend to software monetization.

items: What to say at work: Palantir's 149% US commercial growth is the ultimate counter-argument to the AI bubble thesis. They aren't just selling hype; they are converting tokens into actual, high-margin cash flow.

content.text: SpaceX Tests Gravity: First Earnings Report and a Looming Lock-up Cliff

Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SPCX) is set to report its first-ever quarterly earnings as a public company on Tuesday, August 4, after the close. It has been a brutal start for the stock since its record-setting $75 billion IPO in June: shares have collapsed around 50% from their peak of $225.64 to around $110-114, trading well below the $135 IPO price.

Why does this matter? The IPO was driven by a massive hype cycle surrounding its merger with xAI, pitching SpaceX as an AI infrastructure giant using rockets as a competitive moat. But public markets are now looking at the cold, hard numbers. SpaceX is burning massive cash—spending $40 billion a year on AI infrastructure and its rocket program—and posted a $4.28 billion net loss in Q1. The real headache for investors is the lock-up calendar. On August 6, the first tiered lock-up expires, making up to 911.5 million shares eligible for sale. If insiders decide to cash out, it could trigger a massive wave of selling.

items: What to say at work: SpaceX is finding out that public markets are a lot less forgiving of $40 billion capex bills than private venture capitalists. If Starlink and AI monetization don't show serious acceleration, that $1.4 trillion valuation is going to face some serious gravity, especially with the lock-up expiring this week.

content.text: BP's Fossil Fuel Pivot: Q2 Profits Double as Green Strategy is Dumped

BP reported a blowout Q2 underlying replacement cost profit of $5.73 billion—more than doubling from a year earlier and up 78% from Q1. The results were driven by higher oil prices and strong refining margins. Alongside the earnings, new CEO Meg O'Neill announced a massive portfolio shakeup, including plans to sell its US biogas business Archaea Energy (bought for $4.1 billion in 2022) and its UK North Sea business.

Why does this matter? This is the final nail in the coffin for the green transition strategy championed by previous leadership. BP has written down over $4 billion on low-carbon ventures recently. Under O'Neill, the company is aggressively pivoting back to its highly profitable core oil and gas business to maximize shareholder returns (raising its dividend by 4%). Shareholders are cheering the return of capital, but the windfall profits are drawing political heat.

items: What to say at work: BP dumping Archaea and the North Sea is a textbook example of capital discipline. The market doesn't want oil majors pretending to be utility companies; it wants them pumping oil, cutting costs, and buying back shares.

content.text: US Manufacturing Surges, But the Mood is Miserable

The US ISM Manufacturing PMI rose to 55.6% in July (up from 53.3% in June, beating expectations of 54.0%). This represents the strongest expansion in factory activity since May 2022. Production surged to 58.5%, and employment returned to expansion territory for the first time in 33 months.

Why does this matter? While the headline numbers are booming, the underlying sentiment is surprisingly grim. 62% of panelist comments were negative, with purchasing managers complaining about price volatility, the Iran war, and tariffs. The Prices Paid Index remained highly elevated at 71.1%, showing that input costs are still a major headache. This is a classic good news is bad news scenario for markets. The robust economic expansion gives the Federal Reserve more ammunition to keep interest rates higher for longer.

items: What to say at work: The ISM print shows the economy is running hot, but the supply chain is feeling the squeeze from the Middle East. With prices paid at 71%, anyone expecting the Fed to start slashing rates is dreaming.

content.text: The Trump De-escalation: Oil Tumbles and Wall Street Rallies

On Monday, President Donald Trump called off planned strikes on Iran and announced that new peace talks would begin immediately. This sent Brent crude tumbling over 5% to around $83.24, triggering a massive relief rally on Wall Street. The S&P 500 surged 1.5% to 7,600.50, and the Dow gained 1.3% to set a new record high.

Why does this matter? Geopolitical tensions in the Middle East have been the primary driver of energy price volatility and inflation fears. A sudden de-escalation removes a massive headwind for global equities. While the market is celebrating, macro desks are warning that these de-escalation announcements have collapsed multiple times this year. If the talks fall through, the gap will fill fast, leaving investors exposed to a sudden spike in oil prices.

items: What to say at work: The oil trade broke over the weekend on the Trump headline. It's a great relief rally, but we've seen three of these de-escalations collapse since February. Keep some hedges in place in case the talks fall apart.

content.text: The Morning After: Peace, Pipes, and the Bessent Notepad

If you spent your weekend expecting a geopolitical firestorm in the Middle East, Monday's market was a cold shower of relief. President Trump's decision to hold off on ordering new strikes against Iran—opting instead for immediate peace talks—sent crude oil into a proper tailspin. Brent crude tumbled 4.7% to $83.77 a barrel, while WTI slid over 5% to hover near $80. For a market that spent July sweating over whether energy-driven inflation would get a second wind, this was the ultimate green light.

The relief rally was fast and furious. The S&P 500 jumped 1.48% to close at 7,600.50—putting it a mere whisker (0.1%) off its all-time high. Meanwhile, the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 1.32% to notch its 22nd record close of the year at 53,178.41, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite leaped 2.13%. Lower energy prices and a cooling of Treasury yields (the 10-year fell 5.9 basis points to 4.686%) also gave the rate-sensitive small caps some breathing room, with the Russell 2000 climbing 1.73% to 2,981.91.
The Big Story: The Coordinated Yen Rescue

But the real action wasn't in equities; it was in the FX market, where we saw the first coordinated US-Japan currency intervention since the 2011 earthquake. On Monday, Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama officially confirmed that Tokyo and the US Treasury had stepped in on Friday to buy yen and slap down speculators who had pushed the currency to a 40-year low near 164. The yen surged over 1% to hit an intraday high of 155.20 per dollar before paring some gains to trade around 157-158.

The most amusing detail of the weekend was a classic hot-mic moment: a Reuters photograph of US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's notepad at a Camp David cabinet meeting. Under his To Do list, plain as day, was: 'Buy Japanese Yen $5-10 bil.' Bessent later took to X to support Japan's steps, and Trump chimed in, calling the intervention a 'signal of friendship' (though he couldn't resist a cheeky dig about Pearl Harbor).

Why does this cross-asset move matter to a City desk? Because it's not just about helping a strategic ally. The US stepped in because a collapsing yen was forcing Japan to contemplate dumping its massive holdings of US Treasuries to fund solo interventions. That would have sent US long-term yields—which are already testing 20-year highs, with the 30-year yield touching 5.27% last week—into orbit, destabilising the US public borrowing system. By coordinating, and proposing a Fed repo facility (FIMA) to let Japan swap Treasuries for dollars without selling them, Bessent has managed to put a lid on both USD/JPY and US yields. It's a masterclass in financial self-preservation disguised as diplomacy.
Single-Name & Tech: Oracle's Gemini Glow

On the corporate front, Oracle (ORCL) was the star of the show, jumping 9.22% to $141.85. The database giant is still riding high on its late-July deal to embed Google's Gemini models directly into its Fusion and NetSuite applications. It dragged the rest of the hyperscalers along for the ride: Microsoft rose 4.93%, Alphabet gained 4.88%, and Amazon added 4.58%. When the big boys move like that, the index has no choice but to follow.
Crypto & Commodities: Gold Holds, Bitcoin Catches a Cold

While gold consolidated quietly around the $4,108/oz mark, Bitcoin failed to catch the geopolitical relief wave, slipping 1.2% to trade around $62,400. Crypto was weighed down by a nasty $89 million exploit in the Coldcard hardware wallet firmware. Rather than outright panic-selling, we saw a massive rotation of self-custodied funds back onto centralised exchanges—sending exchange balances to their highest level since April 2025 as retail investors decided that maybe centralised custody isn't so bad after all when your hardware wallet starts leaking.
What's on the Slate Today?

items: JOLTS Job Openings: The June JOLTS report drops today. It's the first major employment indicator of the week and a crucial warm-up act for Friday's Nonfarm Payrolls. If job openings hold up, expect the hawkish Fed camp to feel vindicated.

The Earnings Avalanche: We have a massive cross-sector reporting day. Before the US open, we get numbers from Caterpillar, Pfizer, Merck, Spotify, and BP. After the bell, it's AMD, Amgen, Booking Holdings, and Gilead.

The Yen Fade: Watch USD/JPY closely. Historically, joint interventions trigger a sharp knee-jerk reaction, but the 'post-intervention fade' is a well-worn pattern. Without a structural shift in interest rate differentials (i.e., the BOJ actually hiking or the Fed cutting), speculators will eventually test the authorities' resolve again.

sections.title: Financial Idea of the Day: The Greenshoe Option

content.text: How Banks Short IPOs to Save Them (Risk-Free)

If you have ever watched a highly anticipated IPO debut on the London Stock Exchange or Wall Street, you might notice that the share price often behaves rather weirdly in the first few weeks. It rarely just collapses straight through the floor on day one, even if the company is a bit of a dog. That is not just market efficiency at work; it is the result of some clever financial engineering known as the Greenshoe (or over-allotment) option.

Named after the Green Shoe Manufacturing Company, which first used the structure in 1919, the Greenshoe is a clause in the underwriting agreement that allows investment banks to sell up to 15% more shares than the company originally planned to issue. It is the only legally sanctioned way for underwriters to stabilise a stock's price post-IPO without taking on directional market risk.
The Mechanics: The Beautifully Asymmetric Short

To understand how this works, you have to realise that the syndicate desk (the trading floor team managing the IPO) actually starts day one of trading in a short position. Here is the step-by-step walkthrough:

items: The Base Deal: Let's say a hot new tech firm is IPOing 10 million shares at £10 per share.

The Over-Allotment: The underwriters actually allocate and sell 11.5 million shares to institutional investors at £10. This means the bank has collected £115 million, but they only have 10 million real shares from the company. They are now naked short 1.5 million shares.

Scenario A (The Flop): The stock's listing day is a disaster, and the price drops to £8. To cover their 1.5 million short position, the underwriters go into the open market and buy 1.5 million shares at £8. This massive buying pressure acts as a floor, supporting the stock price. The bank covers its short, pockets a tidy £3 million profit (£10 sale price minus £8 buyback price), and the company's reputation is somewhat spared.

Scenario B (The Pop): The stock is a smash hit and surges to £15. The bank obviously cannot buy shares in the open market at £15 to cover their £10 short without losing £7.5 million. Instead, they exercise their Greenshoe option. They buy the extra 1.5 million shares directly from the issuing company at the original IPO price of £10. They deliver these to the investors, close their short at exactly breakeven, and the company happily pockets an extra £15 million in capital.

content.text: Why This Matters in the City

If you are in asset management, understanding the Greenshoe is vital for pricing IPO participation. It means that for the first 30 days post-listing, there is a massive, artificial buyer of last resort sitting in the market if the stock drops. Once that 30-day window closes and the 'shoe' expires, that safety net vanishes. Many a hedge fund manager has made a tidy sum shorting weak IPOs exactly on day 31.

The classic mistake is thinking that the underwriting bank is taking a massive directional gamble by going short 15% of the deal. In reality, the Greenshoe option makes this short position completely risk-free. The bank has a contractually guaranteed right to buy those shares back at the IPO price from the company. It is a heads-I-win, tails-I-break-even trade for the syndicate desk.
How to Use This in an Interview or Over a Pint

If you are interviewing for an Equity Capital Markets (ECM) or sales and trading role, this is a classic technical question. Walk them through the asymmetric short: 'They over-allocate the book by up to 15%, creating a short position. If the price falls, they buy back in the market to support the price and pocket the spread. If it rises, they exercise the Greenshoe option to buy from the issuer at the offer price, closing the short at breakeven.'

Over a pint with colleagues, you can point to any recent high-profile IPO that has been hovering suspiciously close to its offer price and say: 'Looks like the syndicate desk is working overtime on the Greenshoe to keep that one from breaking issue price. Let's see where it trades in a month when the shoe drops.'

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day

content.text: The Yield Curve VAE: Dynamic Level Injection & No-Arbitrage Neural SDEs

If you have ever tried to train a standard Variational Autoencoder (VAE) on yield curves, you will know it is a bit of a nightmare. Because interest rates globally tend to move up and down together—the classic 'parallel shift' or level factor—the VAE spends about 95% of its latent capacity memorising whether rates are high or low. It completely ignores the subtle, complex twists and turns in the slope and curvature that actually matter for pricing and risk. To make matters worse, standard neural networks have no concept of finance theory; left to their own devices, they will happily generate future yield curves that allow massive, risk-free arbitrage. It is the machine learning equivalent of offering free money at the bar.

A brilliant paper by Fusheng Luo and Helyette Geman (May 2026) solves this with a two-stage, physics-informed architecture. First, they introduce 'Dynamic Level Injection' (CVAEsT+LS). They pick a single maturity—like the 11-year swap rate—as an absolute level anchor. They subtract this anchor from all other tenors before feeding the curve to the encoder. This forces the VAE to focus purely on learning the invariant manifold of relative curve shapes. They also swap the standard Gaussian prior for a heavy-tailed Student-t distribution to handle extreme market shocks (think Liz Truss's mini-budget or sudden central bank panic hikes). Second, they model how this latent shape evolves over time using a continuous-time Neural SDE, strictly penalised by a No-Arbitrage PDE loss.
How it Works in Practice

By separating the absolute level from the relative shape, the model decouples macroeconomic regime dynamics from absolute base rates. When it is time to reconstruct the curve, the absolute level anchor is injected directly back into the decoder. Here is a simplified look at how you would implement the Dynamic Level Injection step in your forward pass:

def forward(yields, anchor_idx):
    level = yields[:, [anchor_idx]]
    relative_yields = yields - level
    z = encoder(relative_yields)
    return decoder(z, level) + level
Why This Matters for the City

If you are a fixed-income quant, a macro portfolio manager, or working in risk management, you are constantly generating synthetic scenarios to stress-test portfolios or price exotic derivatives (like swaptions). Classical models like Heath-Jarrow-Morton (HJM) are mathematically elegant but notoriously brittle in extreme environments, often predicting negative rates or suffering from massive parallel drift. Unconstrained machine learning models, on the other hand, will generate curves with jagged edges and clear arbitrage opportunities. The Luo-Geman framework gives you the best of both worlds: the statistical flexibility of deep learning to capture heavy-tailed, regime-switching dynamics, bound by the strict physical laws of no-arbitrage finance.
The Pub / Interview Talking Point

Next time someone at work complains about neural networks generating unrealistic, arbitrage-violating yield curves, drop this on them: 'The trick is to decouple the absolute base rate from the shape dynamics. If you use Dynamic Level Injection with a Student-t CVAE, you force the latent space to focus purely on the invariant manifold of slope and curvature, while injecting the level anchor directly into the decoder. If you then govern the latent dynamics with a Neural SDE penalised by a No-Arbitrage PDE, you get highly realistic, heavy-tailed scenarios that are guaranteed to be mathematically consistent.' It is an instant way to show you understand both deep generative modelling and the fundamental laws of fixed-income pricing.
The Catch

Nothing in life is free, and this model is no exception. First, choosing the anchor maturity is a hyperparameter choice that can introduce bias; if your anchor tenor (e.g., the 11-year swap) suffers from an idiosyncratic liquidity squeeze, it will distort the entire reconstructed curve. Second, solving a No-Arbitrage PDE penalty inside the training loop of a Neural SDE is computationally brutal. It requires sophisticated adjoint sensitivity methods and can make model calibration painfully slow.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: The Paper
Can LLM-based Financial Investing Strategies Outperform the Market in Long Run? by Weixian Waylon Li, Hyeonjun Kim, Mihai Cucuringu, and Tiejun Ma (KDD 2026 / arXiv:2505.07078).
Why this one?

If you spend any time on LinkedIn or financial Twitter, you've probably seen some breathless thread claiming that GPT-4 is the new Jim Simons. The typical recipe is: feed some news headlines into an LLM, tell it to trade, run a backtest over a cherry-picked six-month period in a bull market, and declare victory. This paper is the ultimate cold shower for that entire narrative. The authors built a rigorous, open-source backtesting framework called FINSABER to test these highly-touted LLM trading strategies over two decades and more than 100 stocks. The results are both hilarious and a massive reality check.
The Gist of It

The researchers took several prominent LLM-based investing agents from recent academic literature and put them through a proper, institutional-grade backtest. To stop the models from 'cheating', they built FINSABER to explicitly eliminate look-ahead bias, account for transaction costs, and—crucially—include delisted stocks to avoid survivorship bias. When subjected to this long-term, cross-sectional test, the supposed 'alpha' of these LLM strategies completely evaporated. But the real gold is in the market regime analysis, which reveals that LLMs behave exactly like the worst kind of retail investor.
Key Takeaways

items: The Bull Market Underperformance: In bull markets, LLM agents are overly conservative. They sit on cash or underperform simple buy-and-hold passive benchmarks because they over-analyse short-term noise and miss the macro trend.

The Bear Market Disaster: In bear markets, they turn into aggressive 'dip buyers'. They suffer from a form of narrative bias, generating beautifully written, highly confident investment theses to justify holding falling knives all the way down, leading to catastrophic losses.

The Complexity Trap: Simply scaling up the complexity of the AI framework—like adding multi-agent debates or deeper memory structures—does not fix the core issue. Without explicit, regime-aware risk controls, you are just paying more in API token costs to lose money faster.

content.text: In Their Own Words

"Systematic backtests over two decades and 100+ symbols reveal that previously reported LLM advantages deteriorate significantly under broader cross-section and over a longer-term evaluation... LLM strategies are overly conservative in bull markets, underperforming passive benchmarks, and overly aggressive in bear markets, incurring heavy losses."
The Sharpe Pint Take

This paper confirms what any sensible quant already suspected: LLMs are brilliant linguists but terrible risk managers. They are trained to be helpful and confident, which is the exact opposite of what you want in a trader. A model that is rewarded for always having a plausible-sounding explanation will happily hallucinate a bull case for a company on its way to bankruptcy. If you are going to use LLMs in asset management, use them for what they are actually good at—extracting structured data from messy earnings calls or regulatory filings. Do not let them touch the execution button. Asking an LLM to time the market is like asking a very eloquent English graduate to fly a Harrier Jump Jet.
What to Say at the Pub (or in an Interview)

items: If someone pitches you a 'revolutionary' AI trading agent, ask them: 'Did you run that through a rolling-window backtest that includes delisted stocks, or are we just looking at survivorship bias over a six-month bull run?'

You can point out that LLMs suffer from a severe lack of regime awareness. They behave like the classic retail investor: too timid when things are going up, and stubbornly catching falling knives when the market turns.

content.text: The Big Muddy: Why We Double Down on Disasters

We have all seen it. A project is clearly circling the drain. The tech integration is a shambles, the client is furious, and the budget has been blown twice over. Yet, the Director who championed it keeps throwing more resources at it, insisting we are 'just around the corner' from a breakthrough. Economists call this the sunk cost fallacy, but psychologists have a much more human name for it: the Escalation of Commitment.

Coined by researcher Barry Staw in his seminal 1976 paper, 'Knee-Deep in the Big Muddy', this bias explains why we do not just throw good money after bad because of the cash already spent—we do it to protect our egos. Staw's key insight was that we are vastly more likely to double down on a failing strategy if we were the ones who made the initial decision. It is not about the money; it is about face-saving and cognitive consistency. Admitting the project is dead means admitting we were wrong, which, in the City, can feel like career suicide.

In finance, this is the portfolio manager who personally pitched a high-conviction stock that has since tanked 40% on terrible earnings. Instead of cutting losses, they write a defensive 20-page memo blaming 'market irrationality' and buy more on the dip. Or the VP who pushed for an expensive, custom CRM system that the team hates, but who keeps hiring expensive consultants to optimise it rather than admitting they should have just bought Salesforce off the shelf.
How you can use this to your advantage

items: The 'New Guy' Test: If you are struggling to let go of a trade, a project, or even a career path, ask yourself: 'If I were hired today to replace myself, would I start this project or buy this asset at today's price?' If the answer is no, you are escalating commitment. Cut it.

Separate the Decider from the Evaluator: If you are running an investment committee or a major project, never let the person who initiated the idea be the sole judge of its ongoing success. Bring in an independent colleague with zero skin in the game to run the post-mortem or review the metrics.

Build a Face-Saving Bridge: If you are managing upwards and need a senior stakeholder to kill a failing project they championed, do not tell them their plan failed. Frame the exit around external factors. Say: 'Your original strategy was spot on for the market in 2024, but macro shifts have changed the playing field. Pivoting now allows us to capture this new opportunity.' Give them an elegant way out.

content.text: One line to remember
We rarely throw good money after bad to save the money; we do it to save our face.
